pages.hook: Parking in American cities can be confusing, because signs give times and rules. A quick look at the sign can save you a big fine.
pages.polite: Ask **“Excuse me, can I park here?”** before you leave your car.

mythfact.s: In most places you cannot park in front of a fire hydrant.
mythfact.why: Fire trucks need access, so cars must keep a distance.

mythfact.s: A parking meter often takes coins, cards or a phone app.
mythfact.why: Many cities allow all three.

mythfact.s: A “no parking” sign means you can stay as long as you like.
mythfact.why: It means you cannot park there at the times shown.

mythfact.s: All parking lots are free in the USA.
mythfact.why: Many lots charge by the hour or day.

compare.br: In Brazil you may see “proibido estacionar” signs, and in some places a guardador helps with parking.
compare.us: In the USA signs show hours and days, and you may pay a meter or a machine.
compare.tip: Read the whole sign from top to bottom. The rule often changes by time or day.
compare.ask: Is parking easy or hard where you live? Say it in English.

quiz.q: A sign says “No Parking.” You can…
Which question asks where to park?
quiz.why: Where can I park? is natural.

pages.title: Reading quest — The wrong spot · part 1
text: Rosa drove around the block three times. It was Saturday, and the streets in Houston were busy. She saw an empty place near a bank and stopped. A man on the sidewalk waved his hand.
“**Excuse me, can I park here?**” Rosa asked. “**No, this is a no parking zone**,” the man said. He pointed to a red sign. Rosa read it: “No Parking, 8 AM to 6 PM.” It was ten o’clock.

“**Where can I park?**” she asked. “**There’s a parking lot on Oak Street**,” the man said. “It’s around the corner.” “**How much is it?**” “**Five dollars an hour**,” he said. “You pay at the machine.”

pages.title: Reading quest — The wrong spot · part 2
text: “**OK. Thanks for the help**,” Rosa said. “**No problem!**” the man answered. “**Drive safe!**” Rosa smiled. She was happy, because a big fine can cost a lot of money.
She drove to Oak Street and found the lot. It was clean and well lit. She parked, took her ticket and put it on the dashboard. Then she walked to the machine and paid for two hours.
Rosa learned something that day: read the sign before you leave the car. A short question can save your day, and your money.
